rationale: The reply disagrees respectfully, uses an analogy with a link to the many named shades of blue to argue that fine-grained labels can be useful, and pushes back on the oppression claim, though "Even you" is a little pointed and the second point has no support.

This reply respectfully pushes back on the parent's self-defense argument with two reasons: owning a gun is riskier to the owner than it helps, and restrictions would raise prices and cut criminals' access. It cites no evidence for either.

The reply is blunt but respectful, and it answers the parent's relevance claim head-on: it separates judging Islam from judging Muslims and argues by analogy that Christian scripture hasn't changed since the crusades, which offers a new, supported counterpoint.
A short, polite question that pushes back on the parent's claim that everyone knows the law, but it makes no explicit claim and adds little support or new information.
The reply is a polite question that challenges an implied accusation, but it is mostly about the exchange between the two users rather than the topic and adds little.

The reply goes after the other user directly ("you are doing a lot of bitching," saying their ancestors shouldn't reap the benefits) and answers each quoted point with sarcastic rebuttals backed by little more than a weak, doubtful Irish example.
The reply insults people outside the conversation (Blanc's followers), which caps civility at 1; it is on topic but gives a bare, unsupported counterpoint that brushes off the parent's example.

The reply respectfully and directly challenges the parent's claim that the fields are easy to compare by asking which simple metric would have comparable studies in both fields; it is phrased as a question, not a supported claim.
The reply is a respectful counterpoint that speaks directly to the thread, but its only support is a brief statement of personal attraction (sex, not gender), so the challenge is thin.

The reply respectfully questions what "better off" means and backs its challenge with specific harms (mental health problems, falling birth rates, less social and family contact) tied to long working hours in East Asia, though it cites no sources.

The reply responds directly by reframing the shop-owner and police prejudice point as evidence of white privilege, which is a little support, but the closing "starting to see" line is a bit condescending and ignores the wage point instead of answering it.

The reply answers each of the parent's examples directly, offers practical alternatives for each one, and clarifies the commenter's position; it is a bit dismissive ("who cares?", "salty bitch") but never attacks the other user.
The reply is a blunt but respectful rebuttal of the EMF cancer claim, backed by a quoted WHO conclusion and a link, so it adds a supported counterpoint.
The reply respectfully answers the parent's sarcastic question head-on, backing its claim with one example (Iranian oil and the British Empire), so the support is real but thin.
The reply answers the question directly and adds a new point, but it calls a group's position "ridiculous" without giving any support for that claim.
The reply is respectful and answers the parent directly by clarifying the goal and asking a question back, but it gives no support for its claims and only adds a little.

This reply is respectful and on topic, and it addresses the hypotheticals by saying leaks are fine when they're true; its only support is the claim that WikiLeaks has a perfect record and a mention of the pay-to-play revelations, and it adds a modest counterpoint plus a personal commitment.

The reply concedes that some of the examples are real, then quotes the exaggerated ones to back up its point, but its closing question ("just emoting?") is condescending toward the other user without being a direct insult.
The reply makes a relevant distinction between foreign and domestic extremism and adds a link, but the 'sit in your own echo chamber' line is condescending and brushes the other user off.

The reply is condescending, with all-caps emphasis and rhetorical questions; it is a tangent about disability expertise that has little to do with the mansplaining thread; it gives one reason (daily experience with disabled people) for its claim; and it mostly restates an earlier point.
The reply explains away an earlier typo, then brushes off the other user with "carry on" and says it reported them, which is dismissive and about the users' dispute rather than the topic.
The reply is a polite, on-topic question that challenges the parent's isolation premise, and it implies a short line of reasoning (more people sharing the bathroom means it is less isolated).

The reply answers the Pulse reference directly and gives one reason (a single incident by a disturbed person doesn't represent all Muslims), but calling the argument bigotry is condescending, and the counterpoint is thin.
The reply respectfully and directly disagrees with the parent, but its only support is personal anecdote ("I have never seen..."), so it offers a counterpoint with limited support.
The reply is respectful and answers both of the parent's questions directly, using the writer's own experience as support, and it adds new information and a concession that the relationship helped.
The reply respectfully disputes the parent's description of the OP by quoting the original post, which gives some support for a relevant counterpoint.
The reply answers the question directly and respectfully, quoting several specific passages from the memo as evidence that it supports diversity, which brings new information into the discussion.
The reply politely admits the user doesn't know enough about the topic and thanks the other person, but it makes no argument and adds nothing new about taxes.

The reply respectfully answers the parent's challenge by defining late stage capitalism and listing specific examples the sub criticizes that it says are unique to that period, though it doesn't explain why each example belongs only to capitalism.

The reply respectfully questions the parent's idea of biological sex, gives its own definition based on hormones and sex characteristics, and asks challenging questions; the definition is only light support for its claim that sex isn't fixed.
The reply is respectful and on topic, and it answers the parent's hypothetical with a boxing counterexample that shows when thanking someone who hit you makes sense.

The reply turns down the parent's point and won't keep talking until its own demand is met, so it's about the fight between the users rather than the topic, gives no support for its claim, and shuts the discussion down, though its tone is curt rather than insulting.
This is a respectful, on-topic reply that suggests a working definition of theft, which moves the debate forward, but it gives no support for that definition.

The reply respectfully clarifies the distinction by giving two thresholds (more likely than not versus beyond reasonable doubt), which adds a fresh way to frame the point, but it gives only a definitional reason as support.
This is a respectful, on-topic clarifying question that asks the other user what they mean by matriarchy and pushes back on that definition, but it makes no claim of its own.

The reply gives a relevant counterexample (the child-abuse analogy), but calling the question "absurdly loaded" and "profoundly ignorant" is condescending toward the argument, and it refuses to discuss whether men face more major equality issues.

The reply talks down to the parent's attitude and calls it a "fuck you got mine mindset" without directly insulting the user, and it gives only a light hypocrisy point to back its claim that this attitude causes harm.
The reply is a sarcastic, dismissive question that calls the other user's views racist without giving support, and it brushes off their concern instead of engaging with it.

The reply is respectful and on topic. It partly agrees with the parent, then adds new points (liberals oppose Citizens United, and some liberals now look back fondly on W. Bush), backed by one example each.
The reply is a bit sarcastic ("a real doozy") but doesn't attack the person, and it answers the parent directly with a reasoned counterpoint: MAGA is a vague slogan, just like the Women's March name.
The reply is a blunt but respectful direct rebuttal that gives one brief reason (forex investors exist) without evidence or elaboration.

The reply responds directly to the parent's point and offers a new counterpoint (working-class control instead of rival billionaires), but it backs this with only a bare assertion that the Kochs are "Super Evil", and that insult targets people outside the conversation, so civility is capped at 1.
The reply is a polite, on-topic expression of confusion that makes no real argument and adds little new to the discussion.

The reply is respectful and builds on the parent's point about doctors owning their practices: it brings in mutualism with a link and asks a challenging question, though its claim that there are many alternatives to capitalism gets only light support.

The reply is somewhat dismissive ("just to push your agenda") and addresses gun bans instead of the parent's false-dichotomy point, giving only thin support (bans will never happen) for a bare counterpoint.
The reply is respectful and on topic: it clears up a misreading, backs its point by contrasting MLK's long track record with Kaepernick's, and asks a hypothetical that challenges the other user.
The reply answers the parent's question directly with one reason (cost), and the hyperbolic price example makes that point mildly sarcastic without attacking anyone.
This reply is respectful and on topic: it disputes the parent's claim about the posts, explains why men are linked to rape as a social issue, and links an example to back up its point.

Calls Kaepernick (outside the conversation) a "nitwit" and mocks the original poster's argument with a parody, which caps civility at 1; it's on topic and gives some support (false dilemma, different times), but it mostly agrees with the parent and adds only a little.
The reply is somewhat dismissive but doesn't attack the user; it says the parent misread the writer's position without explaining or backing that up, and then leaves the conversation.

The reply dismisses the parent's argument as "insipid" with a mocking "lol, what?", which is condescending but aimed at the argument rather than the person, and it clarifies the intended meaning with specific examples of cultural advantages.

The rhetorical question is a bit sarcastic but targets the argument, and it questions the parent's source by pointing out that the beef cuts listed there (organ meats) probably aren't what Peterson meant.

The reply is a respectful, on-topic counterpoint that turns the parent's definition back on the parent, noting that the WNBA excludes men while the NBA is open to women; it adds a new angle, but its support is only one brief inference.
The reply backs up the "just leave" argument with ticket prices and an analogy, but its "seriously?" and boiling-pool image mock the other user's stance without attacking them as a person.

The reply defends the earlier comment by calling the other user's argument absurd, which is dismissive of the argument but not a personal attack; it gives one reason (it was a restatement) but mostly argues about the exchange rather than the topic.
The reply answers each point respectfully, separating the arbitrary age number from the reason consent laws exist, and tests the parent's logic with a murder analogy and a challenging question.

The reply is a respectful clarification and apology that stays on topic and gives a brief reason (the recurring gold-digger framing and family pressure), though it adds little new beyond restating the earlier point.

The reply respectfully takes on the parent's pet-pig example and argues that caring more for a pet, or taking on obligations by adopting one, explains the different treatment without making it inconsistent.
